items: Estimate your cat's expected lifespan using 15 years as a baseline for indoor cats or 12 years for rescue cats with unknown history.
Calculate your total insurance premium cost by multiplying your monthly premium by 12 and then by your cat's estimated remaining years.
Research typical vet costs including routine visits ($150-300), common emergencies ($1,500-3,500), and major emergencies ($3,000-8,000) to build an accurate cost picture.
Compare your total expected vet costs against total premium costs to determine whether insurance is likely to save or cost you money over your cat's lifetime.
Request the breed-specific exclusion list in writing before signing up because some providers exclude hereditary conditions common to your cat's breed.
Check annual coverage caps carefully since a $20,000 cap may not cover your cat's needs if treatment exceeds that amount in one year.
Read the pre-existing condition clause thoroughly and do not rely on verbal explanations from sales representatives about what is and is not covered.
Ask your provider for their rate increase history because most companies raise premiums 15-25% when cats reach age 8 and your actual costs will be much higher than the initial quote.
Look up your provider's claim denial rate through your state insurance department's complaint database to see how often claims are rejected relative to competitors.
Consider self-insuring by depositing your monthly premium equivalent into a high-yield savings account earning 4% APY, which may outperform insurance over time.
Factor in your cat's breed-specific health risks since Persian, Maine Coon, and Siamese cats have known hereditary conditions that affect coverage value.
Verify reimbursement speed by asking current customers about actual payment timelines since provider promises of 5-7 days often differ from real-world experience.
